/your-ultimate-guide-to-becoming-a-real-.title: How to Become a Real Estate Agent in Colorado
/your-ultimate-guide-to-becoming-a-real-.metaDescription: Colorado requires 168 hours of pre-licensing education, a passing exam score, a fingerprint background check, and E&O insurance before you're licensed.

sections.h2: How do you become a real estate agent in Colorado?
paragraphs: In Colorado, you become licensed as a **real estate broker** — the state doesn't have a separate "agent" license tier the way some states do. You need to complete **168 hours** of DORA-approved pre-licensing education, pass both the national and state portions of the Colorado Real Estate Broker's Exam, submit fingerprints for a background check through the Colorado Bureau of Investigation, and carry active errors and omissions (E&O) insurance before your license is issued. That 168-hour requirement is the highest pre-licensing education requirement of any state in the country, according to the [Colorado Division of Real Estate](https://dre.colorado.gov/division-programs/real-estate-broker/education/broker-qualifying-education), so don't let anyone tell you this is a weekend course.

I tell people considering this career: budget real time for the education, not just money. The 168 hours break down into six required courses — Real Estate Law and Practice (48 hours), Colorado Contracts and Regulations (48 hours), Practical Applications (32 hours), Real Estate Closings (24 hours), Trust Accounts and Record-Keeping (8 hours), and Current Legal Issues (8 hours). You can take them online, in person, or through an accredited college, but they all have to come from a DORA-approved provider.

sections.h2: The exam, fingerprints, and E&O insurance
paragraphs: Once you've finished your coursework, you register for the Colorado Real Estate Broker's Exam through PSI, the state's testing vendor. The exam has a national portion and a state-specific portion, and the current [DORA fee schedule](https://dre.colorado.gov/broker-applications-documents-and-fees) lists the broker examination fee at **$44.95**. Exam results are valid for one year from the date you pass each portion, so don't let too much time lapse between passing and applying.

Before you can submit your license application, you also need to complete a fingerprint-based criminal history background check through the Colorado Bureau of Investigation, which cross-checks with the FBI. And every active Colorado broker is required to carry errors and omissions insurance — you need proof of an active policy in place before the state will issue your license, per DORA's [E&O insurance requirements](https://dre.colorado.gov/sites/dre/files/documents/E%26O%20Insurance%20Instructions.pdf). Once all of that is done, the broker license application fee itself is **$83**, according to DORA's current fee schedule — but check that page directly before you budget, since state fees can change.

sections.h2: What nobody tells you about the first year
paragraphs: Getting licensed is the easy part. The harder truth is that Colorado's high education bar filters out a lot of people who aren't serious, but it doesn't guarantee you'll make money in your first year — that comes down to finding a sponsoring broker, building a sphere of business, and being willing to work nights and weekends when your clients are available, not when it's convenient for you.

If you're specifically looking at Northern Colorado — Larimer and Weld counties — the market has its own rhythm compared to Denver: fewer bidding wars in most price ranges lately, a steady base of relocation buyers from out of state, and a strong rental and investment layer around Fort Collins and Colorado State University. I'd rather have this conversation with you directly than have you guess at it from a blog post. If you're weighing brokerages once you're licensed, I can also walk you through [what it's like at LPT Realty](/join-lpt-realty-colorado), which is where I hang my own license.

Colorado's 168-hour requirement is broken into specific courses set by the Division of Real Estate — it's not a single 168-hour block, but a series of required subjects covering real estate law, contracts, practice, closing, current legal issues, and trust accounts, among others. You'll take these through an approved school, either in person or online, and each course has its own exam before you move to the state exam.

After coursework, you sit for the state licensing exam through PSI, the third-party testing vendor DORA uses. You'll also need to clear a criminal background check through fingerprinting with the CBI and FBI, and you'll need errors-and-omissions insurance in place before your license is actually issued — brokerages will typically point you to a group policy so you're not shopping for this alone.

One thing people don't always expect: Colorado licenses brokers, not 'agents' or 'salespersons' the way some states do. Every person practicing real estate here holds a broker's license from day one, even brand new to the business, which is part of why Colorado's education requirement runs so much higher than states with a separate, lighter-weight 'salesperson' tier.

faq: How many hours of education do you need for a Colorado real estate license?

168 hours from a DORA-approved provider, split across six required courses covering law and practice, contracts, practical applications, closings, trust accounts, and current legal issues. This is the highest pre-licensing requirement of any U.S. state.
How much does it cost to get a real estate license in Colorado?

The DORA broker license application fee is $83 and the PSI exam fee is $44.95, according to the Division of Real Estate's current fee schedule. You'll also pay for your 168 hours of coursework and your E&O insurance policy, and those costs vary by provider — confirm current pricing directly with your course provider and insurer.
Do you need a background check to get a Colorado real estate license?
Yes. You must submit fingerprints to the Colorado Bureau of Investigation for a state and national criminal history background check before submitting your license application.
Is E&O insurance required for Colorado real estate brokers?
Yes. Colorado requires every active licensed broker to carry a policy of errors and omissions insurance, and you need proof of active coverage before the state will issue your license.
How long does it take to become a real estate agent in Colorado?

It depends on your pace through the 168 hours of coursework and how quickly you schedule your exam, fingerprinting, and E&O insurance afterward. Many people complete the process in a few months, though it can be faster or slower depending on your schedule.

sections.h2: What homebuying help actually exists for Colorado teachers right now?
paragraphs: The most substantial current program is **CHFA's Schools To Home**, which offers Colorado public school employees — teachers, administrators, counselors, nurses, and support staff — a second mortgage loan of up to **25% of the first mortgage loan amount** to cover down payment and closing costs, according to [CHFA's own program page](https://www.chfainfo.com/single-family-participating-lenders/chfa-schools-to-home-program). It's a shared-appreciation structure: repayment, along with a share of home appreciation, is deferred until you sell, refinance, or pay off the first mortgage. It's open to full-time employees of any Colorado public school, charter school, district, BOCES, or innovation zone, and it cannot be combined with CHFA's other down payment programs.

Separately, CHFA also offers a general **DPA Grant** of up to the lesser of $25,000 or 3% of your first mortgage amount, with no repayment required, and a second-mortgage option up to 4% of the loan at 0% interest, per [CHFA's down payment assistance page](https://www.chfainfo.com/homeownership/down-payment-assistance). These aren't teacher-exclusive, but any first-time Colorado homebuyer, including teachers, can use them, and they can potentially be paired with your first mortgage.

sections.h2: Good Neighbor Next Door — real, but narrow
paragraphs: HUD's **Good Neighbor Next Door** program offers full-time pre-K through 12th grade teachers a **50% discount** off the list price of specific HUD-owned homes located in designated "revitalization areas," according to [HUD's official program page](https://www.hud.gov/program_offices/housing/sfh/reo/goodn). In exchange, you sign a silent second mortgage for the discounted amount and commit to living in the home as your primary residence for 36 months — no interest or payments on that second mortgage as long as you meet the occupancy requirement.

The catch is real: this only applies to specific HUD-owned homes in specific areas, and if more than one qualified buyer bids on the same home, it's awarded by lottery. It's worth checking the HUD Home Store listings if you're a teacher open to a specific location, but I wouldn't build a home search plan around finding one — the inventory is narrow and unpredictable.

sections.h2: A program that's changing, and one I won't recommend
paragraphs: Colorado passed [SB25-167 in 2025](https://www.cohousedems.com/news/signed!-new-law-creates-path-to-homeownership-for-teachers), creating a new **Educator First Home Ownership Program** — a shared-equity down payment assistance program for public school employees, funded through the state's Public School Fund and administered by CHFA, with at least $100 million unlocked by 2028. This is new and still being built out administratively, so ask CHFA directly about current application status before assuming it's live in the exact form described at signing.

I want to be direct about one program you'll see mentioned in older articles: **Landed**, a private company that historically offered down payment support for educators in several states including Colorado. Based on what I can confirm right now, Landed's direct work with Colorado educators appears to have been superseded by the state's new Educator First Home Ownership Program, and I could not verify that Landed is currently accepting new Colorado educator applicants. I'm not going to send you to a program I can't confirm is active — if you're a teacher looking at down payment help, start with CHFA directly and ask what's currently open.

sections.h2: How I'd approach this as your agent
paragraphs: None of these programs work in isolation from your mortgage — CHFA's assistance is always paired with a CHFA first mortgage, so the lender conversation and the agent conversation need to happen together, early. I work with lenders who handle CHFA loans regularly, and I'd rather get you in front of one before you fall in love with a house that doesn't fit the program's price limits.

If you're a Colorado teacher and any of this applies to you, let's talk before you start touring homes — not after. I can also point you toward [first-time homebuyer resources](/first-time-homebuyer) more broadly, since several of these programs overlap with standard first-time buyer requirements.

sections.h2: What I actually recommend, in order
paragraphs: If you're a Colorado educator starting from scratch, I'd start with CHFA directly rather than any third-party site, because their programs are the ones I can verify are currently funded and active, and CHFA can also tell you in one conversation whether the new Educator First Home Ownership Program has opened applications in your area yet. A CHFA-approved lender can run all of this alongside your regular mortgage pre-approval.

From there, ask about stacking: in a lot of cases the CHFA down payment assistance grant can be paired with other CHFA first mortgage products, which is where the real savings usually show up — not from any single program alone, but from combining what you qualify for. That's a conversation for a CHFA-approved loan officer, not something I'd try to estimate for you on a web page.

And if a program you've read about online doesn't show up when your lender or CHFA looks it up, trust that over the blog post. Homebuying program landscapes shift year to year, especially right now with a new state law in play, and the only way to know what's actually available to you today is to ask the agencies administering the money directly.

faq: What is CHFA Schools To Home?

A CHFA program for Colorado public school employees offering a second mortgage loan of up to 25% of your first mortgage amount to help with down payment and closing costs, with repayment deferred and a shared-appreciation component. It's open to full-time employees of any Colorado public school, charter school, district, BOCES, or innovation zone.
Is Good Neighbor Next Door available to Colorado teachers?

Yes, in principle — full-time pre-K through 12th grade teachers can get a 50% discount on specific HUD-owned homes in designated revitalization areas. The limitation is inventory: it only applies to particular HUD-owned properties, and multiple qualified bidders trigger a lottery.
Is Landed still available for Colorado teachers?

I could not confirm that Landed is currently accepting new Colorado educator applicants. Colorado's new Educator First Home Ownership Program, created by state legislation and administered through CHFA, appears to be the current path forward — confirm directly with CHFA before assuming Landed's program is still open.
What is Colorado's new Educator First Home Ownership Program?

A shared-equity down payment assistance program for Colorado public school employees created by state legislation (SB25-167) and administered by CHFA, funded through the state's Public School Fund. It's newer, so confirm current application status directly with CHFA.
Do I need to be a first-time homebuyer to use these teacher programs?

It depends on the program. CHFA's Schools To Home does not require first-time buyer status by itself, but many of CHFA's other down payment assistance products do have first-time buyer or income requirements — check the specific program before assuming you qualify.

/join-lpt-realty-colorado.title: Join LPT Realty in Colorado: What to Know
/join-lpt-realty-colorado.metaDescription: Considering LPT Realty as a Colorado agent? Here's what the compensation model and NoCo market actually look like from someone already on it.

sections.h2: What is it like to join LPT Realty in Colorado?
paragraphs: I'm licensed with **LPT Realty**, and I get asked about it constantly by Colorado agents thinking about switching. The short version: it's a cloud-based national brokerage with no physical offices, built around letting agents choose their own compensation structure rather than locking everyone into one split. For Colorado specifically, that matters because you're not paying for office space you'll never use in Fort Collins or Denver — everything runs through the brokerage's online platform.

LPT operates in all 50 states and has grown fast since launching in 2022, which means there's a real, active agent community here in Colorado, not just a national brand with nobody local. If you're already licensed here — remember, Colorado requires [168 hours of pre-licensing education](/your-ultimate-guide-to-becoming-a-real-estate-agent-in-colorado), among the toughest requirements in the country — the barrier to entry as an agent is already high, and I think that filters for people who take this seriously.

LPT gives you a choice between two plans. The **Business Builder** plan is a flat $500 fee per transaction, capped at $5,000 a year — after that, you're not paying the brokerage anything further on the split side. The **Rev Share Partner** plan is an 80/20 split (you keep 80%) capped at $15,000 a year, and it's the plan that unlocks LPT's revenue-share program, where you can earn a percentage of production from agents you sponsor into the brokerage, distributed across up to seven upline tiers. Both plans carry the same per-transaction and annual fees on top of the split structure. I'd rather you hear the actual mechanics than a recruiting pitch — go review the current numbers directly on [LPT's own site](https://www.lpt.com/) before you commit to a plan, since fee structures can be updated.

For a full breakdown of who each plan suits and who it doesn't, I wrote a separate page on [how LPT's model works in general](/join-lpt-realty) — this page is specifically about doing it here, in Northern Colorado.

I work Larimer and Weld counties — Loveland, Fort Collins, Windsor, Greeley, Eaton, and the smaller towns around them. This isn't Denver. It's a market with a steady base of relocation buyers, a strong rental and investment layer tied to Fort Collins and Colorado State University, and price points that give agents room to build a sustainable book of business without needing to close a luxury deal every month to survive.

If you're a Colorado agent — new or experienced — weighing LPT against a traditional brokerage, I'm happy to talk through what the day-to-day actually looks like here, not just the national numbers. You can also see [what I do for buyers and sellers](/buyers.html) and [/sellers.html](/sellers.html) if you want context on how I run my own business inside this model.

sections.h2: Why the model matters more in a market like this one
paragraphs: Northern Colorado is a market where a lot of agents are part-time, seasonal, or building a book slowly while they figure out their niche. A fee structure that charges you a percentage of every check, win or lose, punishes exactly that kind of ramp-up period. A model built around flat per-transaction fees means a slow month costs you less, and that matters more here than it would in a market where every agent is closing volume every month.

I also think the revenue-share side matters specifically for agents trying to build a team here, because Larimer and Weld counties are growing fast enough that recruiting locally has real upside if the compensation structure rewards you for it. That's a different conversation than 'which brokerage has the best split,' and it's the one I actually want to have with you before you sign anything.

None of this means LPT is the right fit for every agent in this market — some people do better with a traditional brokerage's in-person culture and hands-on manager relationship, and I'd rather tell you that upfront than oversell a model that doesn't match how you like to work.

sections.h2: What to ask before you make the move
paragraphs: If you're currently at a traditional Colorado brokerage and considering a switch, ask your current broker directly what your all-in costs look like over a full year — desk fees, transaction fees, franchise fees, E&O, everything — and compare that total to what a flat-fee model would have actually charged you at your production level. Too many agents compare headline splits without doing that full-cost math, and the real answer is often different from what either brokerage's recruiting pitch would suggest.

I'd also ask about how license transfers work with the Colorado Division of Real Estate, which is a straightforward administrative process but one your new brokerage should walk you through, not leave you to figure out alone. It typically involves an activation form and a brief processing window, and you shouldn't have a gap where you're unable to practice.

faq: Is LPT Realty available to agents in Colorado?
Yes. LPT Realty operates in all 50 states, including Colorado, and has an active agent base in the Northern Colorado market.
What are LPT Realty's commission plans?

Agents choose between a flat $500-per-transaction fee capped at $5,000 a year, or an 80/20 split capped at $15,000 a year that also unlocks revenue share. Both carry additional per-transaction and annual fees — confirm current numbers directly with LPT before deciding.
Do I need a Colorado real estate license before joining LPT Realty?

Yes. You need an active Colorado broker's license, which requires 168 hours of DORA-approved education, a passing exam score, a fingerprint background check, and E&O insurance, regardless of which brokerage you join.
Is LPT Realty a good fit for Northern Colorado agents specifically?

It depends on how you want to build your business. It suits agents comfortable with a cloud-based model and no physical office, who want control over their comp structure. I'm happy to talk through specifics for the Loveland, Fort Collins, Windsor, and Greeley markets.

/dream-home-finder.title: Dream Home Finder: Tell Me What You're Looking For
/dream-home-finder.metaDescription: Describe your ideal Northern Colorado home and I'll match you with listings that fit — no generic auto-alerts, an actual person reviewing it.

sections.h2: What is a dream home finder, and how does this one work?
paragraphs: This is a simple idea: you tell me what you actually want — price range, location, must-haves, deal-breakers — and I use that to search for homes myself, rather than dropping you into a generic auto-alert that emails you every listing within some arbitrary radius. I've had clients get burned by sites that call anything with the right number of bedrooms a "match." A finder is only useful if a person is actually reading what you wrote and filtering with it.

Be specific. "Something nice in Loveland" gets you a stack of listings that technically qualify and mostly don't fit. "Three bedrooms, a fenced yard for the dog, under $500,000, no HOA, within 15 minutes of downtown Loveland" gets you an actual shortlist. The more specific you are about what you don't want, too, the faster I can rule things out instead of sending you homes you'll reject in ten seconds.

sections.h2: What to include when you describe your ideal home
paragraphs: At minimum: your price range (and whether that's flexible), the towns or areas you're open to, must-have features versus nice-to-haves, and your timeline. If you're relocating from out of state, tell me that too — the questions I'd ask a local buyer and an out-of-state relocation buyer are different, and I'd rather ask them up front than waste your time.

If you're not sure yet whether you want Loveland, Fort Collins, Windsor, Greeley, or somewhere smaller, that's a normal starting point — a lot of buyers know their budget and lifestyle before they know their town. I can walk you through the [Larimer](/communities/larimer/loveland.html) and [Weld County](/communities/weld/greeley.html) options and narrow it down together rather than you guessing blind.

I review what you send, and if I have questions before I start searching, I'll ask them rather than sending you a mismatched list just to look responsive. Once I understand what you're after, I'll start sending listings that actually fit — including off-market or coming-soon opportunities when I have them, which don't always show up on public search sites.

This isn't a replacement for touring homes or working with me directly through a purchase — it's the starting point. If you're ready to go further, you can also browse active listings yourself on my [search page](/search-homes.html) or read more about [what buyers should know](/buyers.html) before making an offer in this market.

sections.h2: What happens after you submit your criteria
paragraphs: Once I know your budget, must-haves, and timeline, I set you up on a live search that pulls directly from the same MLS data agents use — not a third-party aggregator running on stale listings. You'll get new matches as they hit the market, not a weekly digest that's already out of date by the time you see it.

I also use that same criteria conversation to flag anything that might complicate a purchase in your target area — HOA rules, well and septic systems in the more rural parts of Larimer and Weld counties, flood zone considerations near certain waterways, that kind of thing. Better to know before you fall for a listing than after you're under contract.

If your search spans both the Denver metro commuter towns and the more rural Northern Colorado communities, I'll say so plainly when a property's location doesn't match what you told me you wanted. The listings that do exist deserve extra scrutiny, and the ones that sound too easy usually are.

sections.h2: Setting realistic search criteria from the start
paragraphs: I'd rather have an honest conversation about budget and inventory upfront than send you on months of tours for homes that were never realistic. Northern Colorado's market moves fast in some price bands and sits stagnant in others, and knowing which segment your search falls into changes how we should approach it — whether that means moving quickly when something comes up or being patient and selective.

If your must-have list and your budget don't currently line up, I'll tell you that directly rather than let you discover it three tours in. Sometimes the fix is a different neighborhood, sometimes it's a different property type, and sometimes it's simply a matter of timing your purchase for when more inventory typically comes on the market.

I also ask new clients to rank their must-haves versus their nice-to-haves before we ever look at a listing together, because almost nobody gets a property that checks every single box at their target price point. Knowing in advance which two or three items are truly non-negotiable — school district, lot size, single-level living, whatever it is for you — makes the whole search faster and a lot less frustrating once real listings start coming in.

faq: How specific should I be when describing my dream home?
As specific as possible. Price range, location, must-haves, deal-breakers, and timeline all help me actually filter listings rather than sending you a generic list. Vague requests get vague results.
Is the dream home finder the same as a generic listing alert?

No. A listing alert emails you anything matching basic criteria automatically. This is me personally reviewing what you describe and searching with that context, including listings that might not be fully public yet.
Do I have to know exactly which town I want before using this?
No. A lot of buyers start with a budget and a lifestyle in mind and figure out the specific town along the way. Tell me what matters to you and we can narrow it down together.
Is there a cost to use the dream home finder?
No — this is part of working with me as your buyer's agent. Tell me what you're looking for and I'll start there.

/the-best-places-to-retire-in-northern-c.title: Best Places to Retire in Northern Colorado
/the-best-places-to-retire-in-northern-c.metaDescription: Loveland, Windsor, Fort Collins, and Greeley each offer something different for retirees — here's the honest comparison, taxes included.

sections.h2: Where should you retire in Northern Colorado?
paragraphs: There isn't one right answer — it depends on what you're optimizing for. **Loveland** offers walkable arts and culture at a moderate price point. **Windsor** sits almost exactly between Fort Collins and Greeley, with newer housing stock, flatter terrain, and active-adult communities already built specifically for retirees. **Fort Collins** gives you the most amenities, medical care, and university-town energy, generally at the highest price. **Greeley** is the most affordable of the four and still gives you reasonable access to everything else in the region.

I tell retiring clients to start with the trade-off, not the town: do you want walkability and culture, or do you want the lowest possible cost of living with a short drive to everything else? Once you answer that, the town usually picks itself.

Colorado has a flat state income tax and offers a real benefit for retirees: a pension and annuity subtraction. If you're **55 to 64**, you can subtract up to **$20,000** of qualifying pension, annuity, and retirement account income from your Colorado taxable income. If you're **65 or older**, that subtraction increases to **$24,000**, according to the [Colorado Department of Revenue](https://tax.colorado.gov/income-tax-topics-social-security-pensions-and-annuities). These are per-person limits, so a married couple who both qualify can potentially double them on a joint return.

Social Security treatment has also become more favorable in recent years for many taxpayers — check the [Colorado Department of Revenue's retiree page](https://tax.colorado.gov/retirees) directly for the current rules that apply to your age and income, since eligibility depends on your specific situation and the rules have been changing.

sections.h2: Property taxes and the honest cost-of-living picture
paragraphs: Here's the good news: Colorado's property taxes are genuinely low by national standards, with an effective rate around 0.5% of assessed value — well below most states. On top of that, homeowners **65 and older** who've owned and occupied their home for at least 10 consecutive years may qualify for the state's senior property tax exemption, which exempts 50% of the first $200,000 of a home's actual value, according to the [Colorado Division of Property Taxation](https://dpt.colorado.gov/property-tax-exemption-for-senior-citizens-in-colorado). That's a meaningful break if you've been in your home a long time.

Now the honest part: low property taxes don't mean low cost of living overall. Colorado's home values and general cost of living run above the national average, and Northern Colorado has gotten more expensive over the last several years as more people have moved here. If you're relocating from a state with a much lower cost of living, do the full math — housing price, property tax, income tax subtraction, and day-to-day costs — before assuming Colorado is automatically a savings compared to where you are now.

sections.h2: What I'd actually tell you if you asked me directly
paragraphs: If you want walkable and cultured, look hard at [Loveland](/communities/larimer/loveland.html). If you want new construction and active-adult community options with flat, easy terrain, look at [Windsor](/communities/weld/windsor.html) — there are already 55+ communities built there. If budget is your top priority, [Greeley](/communities/weld/greeley.html) stretches further than the others. And if you want to be close to the most doctors, specialists, and amenities as you age, [Fort Collins](/communities/larimer/fort-collins.html) is worth the premium for a lot of people.

None of these are wrong choices. They're different trade-offs, and I'd rather walk you through your specific situation — income, mobility needs, family nearby — than hand you a generic ranked list. Reach out through my [contact page](/contact.html) and let's actually talk it through.

sections.h2: Questions I ask retiring clients before we tour anything
paragraphs: How often do you plan to fly out of Denver International, and does an extra 30-45 minutes of drive time bother you? That single question rules towns in or out for a lot of retirees faster than anything else we discuss, especially those weighing Windsor or Eaton against something closer to the metro area.

Do you want single-level living now, even if you don't need it yet? A surprising number of retirees buy a two-story home because it's what they've always had, then end up selling five years later once stairs become a daily hassle. It's worth deciding upfront whether you're buying for today or for the next 15-20 years.

And how much winter maintenance are you actually willing to do? Northern Colorado gets real snow, and a lot of retirees underestimate how much shoveling, roof-raking, and general upkeep a larger property demands compared to a smaller lot or a maintenance-included community.

faq: What is the best town to retire in Northern Colorado?

It depends on your priorities. Loveland suits retirees who want walkable arts and culture, Windsor suits those wanting newer housing and active-adult communities, Fort Collins offers the most amenities and medical care, and Greeley is the most affordable option.
Does Colorado tax retirement income?

Yes, but with a significant subtraction. Taxpayers 55-64 can subtract up to $20,000 of qualifying pension and retirement income, and those 65+ can subtract up to $24,000, per the Colorado Department of Revenue. Social Security treatment varies by age and income — check the state's current rules directly.
Are property taxes low in Colorado for retirees?

Yes, relatively. Colorado's effective property tax rate is around 0.5%, among the lowest in the country, and homeowners 65+ who've owned and lived in their home for 10+ years may qualify for a senior exemption on 50% of the first $200,000 of home value.
Is Northern Colorado affordable for retirees compared to the rest of the state?

It varies by town. Greeley tends to be the most affordable of the major Northern Colorado towns, while Fort Collins runs highest. All of them sit within Colorado's above-average overall cost of living, so it's worth running the full numbers for your situation.

/join-lpt-realty.title: How LPT Realty's Compensation Model Works
/join-lpt-realty.metaDescription: LPT Realty offers agents a choice: an 80/20 split capped at $15,000, or a flat $500-per-transaction fee capped at $5,000. Here's who each suits.

sections.h2: How does LPT Realty's compensation model actually work?
paragraphs: LPT Realty gives agents a choice between two compensation plans instead of locking everyone into one structure. The **Rev Share Partner plan** is an 80/20 split — you keep 80% of your commission — capped at **$15,000** a year in company dollar. Once you hit that cap, you keep essentially all of your commission (minus a standard per-transaction fee) for the rest of your anniversary year. The **Business Builder plan** is a flat **$500 fee per transaction**, capped at **$5,000** a year, with no percentage split at all — after ten transactions' worth of fees, you're capped and paying only the standard per-transaction fee going forward. Both plans carry the same additional annual and per-transaction fees on top of the split structure. I'd point you to [LPT's own site](https://www.lpt.com/) for the current exact numbers before you commit, since brokerage fee structures do get updated.

The Rev Share plan is the one that unlocks LPT's revenue-share program: agents who sponsor other agents into the brokerage can earn a percentage of what those agents produce, distributed across up to seven upline tiers. Business Builder agents don't participate in revenue share. That's the core trade-off — Business Builder is simpler and more predictable, Rev Share Partner has a higher ceiling if you're actively building a team or recruiting.

sections.h2: Who this suits — and who it doesn't
paragraphs: Business Builder tends to suit agents who want a straightforward, predictable cost structure and don't plan to recruit or build a downline. If you're closing a handful of deals a year and don't want to think about revenue-share math, the flat fee is easier to plan around. It's also a reasonable starting point for newer agents who aren't sure yet whether team-building is part of their long-term plan.

Rev Share Partner suits agents who are actively building a business beyond their own transactions — recruiting other agents, building a team, or aiming for the kind of income that comes from more than closing deals yourself. It costs more if you're not using the revenue-share side of it, so I wouldn't recommend it just because it sounds more sophisticated. Match the plan to what you're actually doing, not what sounds more ambitious.

sections.h2: What LPT is, structurally, if you're comparing brokerages
paragraphs: LPT is a cloud-based brokerage with no physical offices, which is part of why it can offer flexible comp plans without the overhead of brick-and-mortar locations. It launched as a brokerage in 2022 and has grown quickly, now operating in all 50 states. If you're comparing it against a traditional local brokerage, the biggest cultural difference is that there's no office to walk into — everything from training to support runs through the company's online platform.

If you're specifically a Colorado agent weighing this, I wrote a companion page on [what joining LPT looks like here in Northern Colorado](/join-lpt-realty-colorado) specifically — the market dynamics, the licensing requirements, and what it's actually like day-to-day in this region.

sections.h2: Who this model tends to suit, and who it doesn't
paragraphs: Agents who do well under a cloud-brokerage, flat-fee structure tend to be self-directed: they don't need daily walk-in access to a manager's office, they're comfortable building their own systems, and they've already got some base of business or a clear plan to generate one. If that's not you yet, that's not a knock — it just means a more traditional, in-person brokerage with hands-on floor time might get you further, faster, while you're building your foundation.

Teams and producing agents who've outgrown a percentage-of-every-check split tend to be the ones who benefit most from a flat, capped fee structure, because the math favors volume. If you're closing one or two deals a year while you keep a separate day job, the annual fees might be a bigger relative bite than a traditional split would be — that's worth running the actual numbers on before you switch.

I'd rather walk you through the real math for your specific production level than give you a generic pitch. Bring me your last 12 months of closed volume and let's see what the two structures would have actually cost you.

sections.h2: How the revenue share side actually works
paragraphs: Beyond the per-transaction and annual fee structure, LPT's revenue share is built around a multi-tier system tied to agents you personally sponsor into the brokerage, and their production. It's not guaranteed income, and it's not something that pays off quickly — it's a longer-term structure that rewards agents who are actively building a network, not agents who join and stay passive.

If revenue share isn't something you're interested in building, that's fine — the Business Builder track lets you opt out of that entirely and just pay the flat per-transaction fee up to the annual cap, which is a simpler and more predictable structure for agents who just want to close deals without also recruiting.

faq: What are LPT Realty's two compensation plans?

An 80/20 split capped at $15,000 a year (Rev Share Partner), and a flat $500-per-transaction fee capped at $5,000 a year (Business Builder). Both carry additional standard fees — confirm current numbers directly with LPT.
Which LPT Realty plan is better for a new agent?

It depends on your goals, not your experience level. Business Builder is simpler and more predictable if you're not planning to recruit. Rev Share Partner makes more sense if you intend to build a team or actively recruit other agents, since it's the plan that unlocks revenue share.
Does LPT Realty have physical offices?
No. LPT operates as a cloud-based brokerage with no brick-and-mortar offices, which is part of how it supports flexible compensation plans without traditional office overhead.
Can I switch between LPT Realty's compensation plans?
Brokerages that offer plan choices typically have specific rules and waiting periods for switching between them. Confirm the current policy directly with LPT before assuming you can switch freely.

/coaching-for-real-estate-agents.title: Real Estate Agent Coaching & Mentorship
/coaching-for-real-estate-agents.metaDescription: Coaching for real estate agents who want direct, honest feedback on their business — not generic scripts. Here's how I approach it.

sections.h2: What does real estate agent coaching actually involve?
paragraphs: Good coaching isn't handing you a script and a motivational poster. It's looking at your actual business — your lead sources, your conversion rates, how you're spending your time — and being honest about what's working and what isn't. I tell agents I coach the same thing I tell buyers and sellers: uncomfortable truths early save you months of wasted effort later. If your follow-up process is the problem, no amount of new leads fixes it.

For newer agents specifically, a lot of coaching is just filling in what licensing school doesn't teach you: how to actually generate business, how to structure your day, how to talk to a seller who's nervous about pricing, and how to handle the stretches — and there will be stretches — where nothing seems to be closing.

sections.h2: Who this is for, and who it isn't
paragraphs: This is for agents who are licensed and want to build a real, sustainable business — not people looking for a guaranteed script that replaces actual work. I've coached agents at very different stages: brand new and unsure where to start, and a few years in but plateaued because the habits that got them started stopped scaling.

It's probably not for you if you're looking for passive income promises or a system that removes the need to talk to people directly. Real estate, at every level, is still a relationship business, and coaching should sharpen how you build and manage those relationships — not pretend you can automate your way past that.

I ask about your actual numbers before I offer opinions — what's your lead source, what's your close rate, where are deals falling apart. Vague goals get vague coaching. Specific numbers get specific, actionable feedback. If you're already at a brokerage and considering a change, I'm also happy to talk honestly about what different comp structures and support systems actually look like day-to-day — including [what it's like at LPT Realty](/join-lpt-realty), which is where I'm licensed.

If you're a licensed Colorado agent — new or a few years in — and you want a direct conversation about where your business actually stands, reach out through my [contact page](/contact.html) and tell me specifically what's not working. That's the fastest way to get something useful out of this rather than a generic first call.

Most agents who reach out to me are stuck on one of a few things: lead generation that isn't converting, a pipeline that's inconsistent month to month, or a business that's grown past what they can manage with their current systems. We start by figuring out which of those is the real bottleneck, because the fix is different for each one, and a lot of agents are trying to solve a conversion problem with more leads when the actual issue is follow-up.

I built a lot of my own systems by necessity, running expired-listing and luxury niches in a competitive Colorado market, then building out the technology and team structure to support it. That's the lens I coach from: what actually moved the needle for a real business, not a theoretical framework. If you're building a team, I can also help you think through delegation and hiring in a way that doesn't just add overhead.

sections.h2: What coaching with me is not
paragraphs: I'm not going to hand you a generic script package or a canned social media calendar and call it coaching — you can find that anywhere, and it rarely produces results because it isn't built around your actual market or your actual strengths. What I do instead is look at what's already working in your business, even in small amounts, and figure out how to do more of that specifically.

This also isn't a fit for agents looking for a passive membership or a course to binge once and forget. It works best for agents who want direct, ongoing feedback on real numbers and are willing to actually implement changes between conversations, not just collect advice.

I'll also tell you honestly if I don't think coaching is what you need right now. Sometimes an agent's real problem is a brokerage mismatch, a burnout issue, or a market they've outgrown, and no amount of coaching fixes that — changing the underlying situation does. I'd rather have that direct conversation upfront than take you on as a client for a problem coaching can't actually solve.

faq: What does real estate coaching for agents typically cover?
Lead generation, conversion and follow-up, time management, negotiation and client conversations, and business planning. Good coaching starts from your actual numbers, not generic scripts.
Is agent coaching only for brand-new real estate agents?
No. It's useful for new agents figuring out where to start, and just as useful for agents a few years in who've plateaued because habits that worked early stopped scaling.
How is real estate coaching different from a brokerage's standard training?

Brokerage training is usually general and one-size-fits-all. Coaching that actually works looks at your specific business — your numbers, your market, your bottlenecks — and gives feedback tailored to that.
Do I need to be at a specific brokerage to get coaching from you?
No. This conversation is about your business and your growth, regardless of where you're currently licensed.

/buyers-or-sellers-market.metaDescription: Is Northern Colorado a buyer's market or a seller's market in 2026? The honest, sourced answer — by county, by property type, and what it means if you're buying or selling.
intro: Ask five people whether Northern Colorado is a buyer's market or a seller's market right now and you'll get five different answers — and honestly, they might all be right. As of mid-to-late summer 2026, the [Colorado Association of REALTORS®](https://coloradorealtors.com/2026/08/12/colorado-housing-market-holds-steady-but-growing-divide-emerges-between-single-family-and-attached-homes/) describes Weld County as "moving toward a more balanced and measured market," with the county's median sale price at $500,000 in July 2026, down 2.7% year-over-year — while Fort Collins single-family homes bucked that trend entirely, posting a median sale price of $640,000, up 6.7% year-over-year over the same period.

The honest answer is: it depends what you're buying and where. Attached homes and condos have softened noticeably almost everywhere — Fort Collins condos and townhomes are running roughly 100 days on market, well above the single-family pace — while well-priced single-family homes under $600,000 still move quickly and can draw multiple offers. Mortgage rates are part of the story too: [Freddie Mac](https://www.freddiemac.com/pmms) put the 30-year fixed average at 6.65% as of August 20, 2026, down slightly from a 2026 high of 6.69% earlier that month, per [Realtor.com](https://www.realtor.com/research/freddie-mac-mortgage-rates-august-06-2026/).

paragraphs: Balanced doesn't mean nothing is happening — it means neither side has all the leverage. [CAR's July 2026 report](https://coloradorealtors.com/2026/07/14/colorados-housing-market-remains-steady-as-summer-buying-season-settles-into-more-balanced-rhythm/) described Fort Collins as "generally balanced between buyers and sellers," with single-family days on market at 62 and slowly declining. Weld County's months of supply dropped to 3.3 in July 2026 (down from 3.7), and average days on market fell to 54 (down from 60) — both signs the market is tightening a bit even while prices in that county stay flat to slightly down.

Redfin's town-by-town numbers tell a similarly mixed story for the three months ending June 2026: Loveland's median sale price rose a modest 0.6% to about $498,000, Greeley's dipped 1.0% to roughly $428,000, and Weld County overall was down 3.2% to about $489,000. None of these moves are dramatic — this is a market recalibrating, not one that's crashing or overheating.

sections.h2: What This Means If You're Buying
paragraphs: More selection, more room to negotiate on inspection items and closing costs, and less pressure to waive contingencies just to compete — especially on anything that's been sitting 45+ days. That doesn't mean every home is a deal; well-priced, well-located single-family homes under $600,000 are still moving in the 50-60 day range and can still see competing offers.

The bigger factor for most buyers right now is the mortgage rate, not the price. At 6.65% as of August 20, 2026 ([Freddie Mac](https://www.freddiemac.com/pmms)), payment math matters more than headlines about the market — which is exactly why I walk every buyer through real numbers on a specific house instead of general market talk.

sections.h2: What This Means If You're Selling
paragraphs: Pricing and presentation matter more than they did during the pandemic years. [CAR's August 2026 report](https://coloradorealtors.com/2026/08/12/colorado-housing-market-holds-steady-but-growing-divide-emerges-between-single-family-and-attached-homes/) put it plainly: "buyers were becoming more selective and sellers needed strategic pricing and presentation." That's especially true for attached homes and condos, which are sitting on the market noticeably longer than single-family houses right now.

It's not a discouraging market to sell in — it's a market where the first two weeks matter. A home priced to reflect current comps and shown well from day one is still selling in weeks, not months, in most Northern Colorado towns.

faq: Is Northern Colorado a buyer's market or a seller's market in 2026?

Neither, cleanly. The most consistent read from the Colorado Association of REALTORS® is a market that's balanced overall, with single-family homes under $600,000 still leaning slightly toward sellers and attached or condo product favoring buyers. It's genuinely property-type and price-band dependent.
Are home prices going up or down in Northern Colorado right now?

Both, depending on where you look. Weld County's median sale price was down 2.7% year-over-year in July 2026 while Fort Collins single-family homes were up 6.7% over the same period, per CAR. Redfin's city-level numbers for Loveland, Greeley, and Weld County show smaller moves in both directions — this isn't a market moving sharply in one direction.
Should I wait for mortgage rates to drop before buying?

It depends on your timeline. Rates have hovered in the mid-6% range through most of 2026 (6.65% as of August 20, 2026, per Freddie Mac), and Fannie Mae's own August 2026 forecast expects them near 6.8% through the end of the year and into 2027 — so waiting for lower rates may mean waiting through more than one buying season.
How long are homes taking to sell in Northern Colorado?

It varies by town: Redfin puts Fort Collins at 47-48 days, Loveland at 53 days, Greeley at 54 days, and Weld County at 54 days on average, all as of data through June 2026 — up modestly from the prior year almost everywhere, consistent with a market that's cooled slightly from its peak pace.

/west-greeley.metaDescription: West Greeley home prices, new-construction subdivisions, schools, and the $1.1B Westside Project — everything to know about this growing side of Greeley, Colorado.
intro: West Greeley has quietly become one of the more active growth corridors in Northern Colorado. [Redfin](https://www.redfin.com/neighborhood/352187/CO/Greeley/West-Greeley) tracks it as its own distinct submarket — covering areas like Southwest Nashua, Southeast Nashua, Water Valley, Edwards, and Cascade Park — with a median sale price of $465,645 as of June 2026, down 2.0% year-over-year, running somewhat above [Greeley's citywide median](https://www.redfin.com/city/8215/CO/Greeley/housing-market) of roughly $428,000 over the same period.

New construction has picked up noticeably along the U.S. Highway 34 corridor on the west side, in subdivisions like Union Colony West, The Cache, Lake Bluff, and Poudre Heights, with early pricing in the $417,000–$518,000 range according to [2025 Greeley Tribune reporting](https://edition.pagesuite.com/tribune/article_popover.aspx?guid=f809d2d1-e320-497f-83c9-1bc0d22ebc2b) on the area. [See current West Greeley listings](/search-homes.html?cities=Greeley&noFloor=true) to compare what's actually on the market today.

paragraphs: The west side is home to [Greeley West High School](https://www.greeleyschools.org/schools) (2401 35th Avenue) and sits adjacent to the [University of Northern Colorado's West Campus](https://www.unco.edu/campus-life/our-campus/), home to several of UNC's colleges. Families also have the city's [Family FunPlex](https://greeleygov.com/activities/recreation/facilities/family-funplex), a major recreation facility at 1501 65th Avenue, and everyday shopping at Westlake Shopping Center, anchored by a King Soopers.

sections.h2: The Westside Project (“Cascadia”): Why West Greeley Is Worth Watching
paragraphs: The biggest story shaping this side of town is the [Greeley Westside Project](https://www.greeleywestsideproject.com/) — a roughly 300-acre, $1.1 billion mixed-use development approved by Greeley City Council that will include an 8,600-seat arena (the new home of the Colorado Eagles hockey team), a year-round indoor water park and resort, a conference hotel, and as many as 11,000 planned housing units, per the project's own materials. Design and construction were expected to run through 2026, with the arena and water park targeted for completion by mid-2028, according to [Denver7](https://www.denver7.com/news/front-range/greeley/greeley-city-council-to-vote-on-proposed-1-1b-entertainment-district-featuring-arena-water-park-hotel).

For buyers weighing west versus east Greeley, that combination — active new-construction subdivisions, UNC's West Campus, and a major entertainment district taking shape nearby — is the clearest reason the west side keeps coming up in conversations about where to buy next.

faq: What is considered West Greeley?

West Greeley generally covers the area along and beyond 10th Street/U.S. Highway 34 toward Windsor and Loveland, in and around the 80634 zip code — including neighborhoods like Southwest Nashua, Water Valley, Cascade Park, and newer subdivisions such as Union Colony West and Lake Bluff.
How much do homes cost in West Greeley?

Redfin puts the West Greeley median sale price at $465,645 as of June 2026, down 2.0% year-over-year — somewhat above Greeley's citywide median of roughly $428,000. New-construction homes in west-side subdivisions have listed from around $417,000 to $518,000.
What is the Greeley Westside Project?

Also called “Cascadia,” it's a $1.1 billion, 300-acre entertainment and housing development approved in 2025 that will include an 8,600-seat arena for the Colorado Eagles hockey team, an indoor water park, a conference hotel, and up to 11,000 planned housing units, with construction expected through 2026 and the first phase targeted for mid-2028.
Is West Greeley a good place to buy right now?

It's one of the more active growth areas in Northern Colorado right now, with real new-construction activity and a major entertainment district in the pipeline — worth a serious look if you want to be early to an area before its next wave of amenities lands.

/ault-summer-festival-coming-this-weeken.metaDescription: The Ault Fall Festival is a Weld County tradition each August at Liberty Park — food, a parade, car shows, a beer garden and fireworks. What to know, and what it says about calling Ault home.
intro: Despite this page's URL, the town's real event is called the **Ault Fall Festival** — ironically named, since it happens in the middle of summer, not the fall. The [Town of Ault's own website](https://www.aultcolorado.gov/events) lists Liberty Park, at 1st Avenue and 1st Street, as the festival's home.

Multiple sources describe it consistently: [Uncover Colorado](https://www.uncovercolorado.com/towns/ault/) puts it on "the first weekend in August" every year, and [The Group Real Estate's](https://thegroupinc.com/uncategorized/things-to-do-in-ault-colorado/) community guide describes food vendors, a beer garden, fireworks, car shows, a parade, and more. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ault,_Colorado) notes it also includes contests and a street dance — small-town Colorado, done right.

A festival was still very much happening in Ault as recently as August 2026 — [Denver7 reported](https://www.denver7.com/news/eastern-plains/microburst-injures-ault-vendor-raises-questions-about-increasingly-severe-winds) on a microburst that tore through a festival there the weekend before its August 11, 2026 story ran, injuring a vendor. No official source has published an exact date for this year's event, so check the [Town of Ault's own site](https://www.aultcolorado.gov/events) closer to early August for the confirmed schedule.

sections.h2: What Living Near Ault Is Actually Like
paragraphs: Ault is a small Weld County town that leans into its own community events — alongside the Fall Festival, it also hosts an International Food Fest each late September. If you're weighing whether a small town like Ault fits your lifestyle, this kind of calendar — where the whole town shows up for the parade and the fireworks — is a real part of the answer, not just a nice-to-have.

sections.h2: Thinking About Buying In Ault Or Nearby?
paragraphs: Ault sits in the same corridor as Eaton, Nunn, and the rest of eastern Weld County — communities where a festival calendar like this one is exactly what draws people who want small-town pace without giving up Northern Colorado access. I can send you what's currently for sale in and around Ault, or answer honestly whether it fits what you're looking for.

faq: What is the Ault Fall Festival?

It's Ault, Colorado's signature annual community festival, held at Liberty Park with food vendors, a parade, car shows, a beer garden, fireworks, and a street dance. Despite the name, it happens in the summer, not the fall — a long-running local joke about the name.
When is the Ault Fall Festival?

It's traditionally held the first weekend in August, though no official source publishes a fixed calendar date months in advance. Check the Town of Ault's own website or Facebook page as the date approaches for the confirmed schedule.
Is the Ault Fall Festival still happening?
Yes — a town festival in Ault was still active as of August 2026, per local news coverage of a weather incident at that year's event. It remains an active community tradition.

paragraphs: Eaton is a Weld County town of about 6,000 people, twelve miles east of Fort Collins. Strong school district (Eaton RE-2), a small but real downtown, and both established and new-build neighborhoods on the west and north edges.

sections.h2: The Housing Story In Eaton For Sale
paragraphs: Eaton, Colorado, is a welcoming agricultural town with a rich history and a strong sense of community. Located just north of Greeley, it offers a peaceful, small-town lifestyle surrounded by Colorado’s scenic beauty. Known for its excellent schools and family-friendly atmosphere, Eaton is an ideal place to enjoy a quiet and fulfilling way of life.
About 9 miles / roughly 15-17 minutes to Greeley via US-85, Eaton's primary job center.

Fort Collins is the largest city in Northern Colorado and the anchor of the region — CSU, the Old Town district, and a housing market that's consistently competitive. Buyers here have to decide between the historic core, the Harmony corridor's newer executive neighborhoods, and everything in between.

sections.h2: The Housing Story In Fort Collins For Sale
paragraphs: Fort Collins is a vibrant and welcoming city in Northern Colorado, set at the foothills of the Rocky Mountains. Known for its thriving craft beer scene, top-rated schools, and abundant outdoor recreation, it offers the perfect balance of small-town charm and big-city amenities. The city features tree-lined streets with historic homes, modern new-build communities, and stunning luxury properties.
About 64 miles / roughly 1 hour 17 minutes to Denver via I-25 (longer with typical traffic); about 20 miles / 37 minutes to Berthoud, and roughly 10 miles to Timnath.

Loveland is where Christine lives and works — the 'Sweetheart City' between Fort Collins and Longmont, with Boyd Lake, the Big Thompson River corridor, and a real downtown. Housing stock is genuinely mixed here: historic bungalows west of Wilson, mid-century ranches in the middle, and newer subdivisions along Boyd Lake and out toward the Ranch.

sections.h2: The Housing Story In Loveland, CO For Sale
paragraphs: Loveland, Colorado, is a charming city celebrated for its artistic vibe, scenic beauty, and warm community spirit. Near the Rocky Mountains, it offers stunning landscapes, a rich arts scene, and a range of opportunities for outdoor adventures. Known as the “Sweetheart City,” Loveland blends creativity and nature seamlessly, making it a unique and inviting place to live.
About 51 miles / roughly 1 hour 4 minutes to Denver via I-25; about 33 miles / roughly 49 minutes to Boulder via CO-119.
Carr is a Weld County crossroads north of Nunn, right up against the north edge of Weld County. It's ranch country and Pawnee National Grassland edge — buyers here want land, a well, and no HOA.

Carr is an unincorporated community in far northern Weld County, settled in 1872 and sitting almost exactly halfway between Fort Collins and Cheyenne — 32 miles to the first, 22 to the second. Nobody buys in Carr for the town, and it would be strange to pretend otherwise: what is here is a church, the old schoolhouse, a scatter of houses, and land. A great deal of land, with nothing between it and the Front Range but sky.

32 miles to Fort Collins and 22 miles to Cheyenne, with I-25 reached via County Road 126. Carr is the closest community to the halfway point between those two cities, which is the practical case for living here: two Front Range job markets inside a half-hour each. Be clear-eyed about the school run, though — Highland's schools are in Ault, and Weld RE-9's bus routes cover 539 square miles for a reason.

Aspen Meadows is a mid-2000s master-planned neighborhood on the north side of Eaton, off County Road 74. Ranch and two-story homes on typical suburban lots, most built between 2004 and 2018 — this isn't rural acreage, it's a walkable subdivision with sidewalks, a park, and a school bus loop.

sections.h2: The Housing Story In Aspen Meadows
paragraphs: Most Aspen Meadows homes are 3–5 bedrooms, 1,800–3,200 finished square feet, with either an attached two-car or three-car garage. HOA is modest and covers the entrance, the park, and a few common landscaping strips — no pool or clubhouse. Metro district status matters here — some phases carry additional taxes; ask before you offer.

If you're weighing Aspen Meadows against similar Eaton or Severance subdivisions, the honest differentiator is the school assignment (Eaton RE-2 is one of the reasons families move here) and how close you want to be to the tech and manufacturing employers in Windsor, Greeley, and Fort Collins. I've sold homes on both sides of that comparison — happy to talk through it before you're locked into a search.

Ault is small — a Weld County town of about 1,900 people, twenty minutes north of Greeley on Highway 85. Buyers here are usually looking for room, quiet, and a shorter commute to the Weld County oilfield or ag jobs than they'd get from Fort Collins.

Ault is a small, close-knit agricultural town in Weld County, sitting along US Highway 85 just a few miles north of Eaton and about 12 miles north of Greeley. Founded in 1904, Ault has held onto its farming roots even as the broader Front Range grows up around it. It's the kind of place where Main Street antique shops, a slower rhythm, and open prairie views still define daily life, and where neighbors genuinely know each other.
About 12 miles / roughly 15-18 minutes to Greeley via US-85, Ault's nearest job center.

Berthoud sits between Loveland and Longmont on Highway 287 — a small town that's grown fast in the last decade as families and remote workers look for something quieter than either neighbor. New subdivisions on the east side, older Craftsman and ranch homes near the historic core.

Berthoud, Colorado, is a picturesque town often called the “Garden Spot of Colorado” for its lush landscapes and tree-lined streets. Between Longmont and Loveland, it combines small-town charm with stunning views of the Rocky Mountains. Known for its tight-knit community, Berthoud offers a welcoming atmosphere, historic character, and a love for outdoor living, making it a truly special place to call home.
About 7 miles (12 min) to Loveland, 20 miles (37 min) to Fort Collins via US-287, and roughly 46 miles (about 56 min) to Denver via I-25.

Eaton Commons is a newer subdivision on the west edge of Eaton — early 2010s through current phases, still building out in spots. Ranches, two-stories, some patio homes on smaller lots designed for lower maintenance. The neighborhood sits close to Eaton Country Club and the town's main north-south corridor (Highway 85's frontage is a few blocks east).

sections.h2: The Housing Story In Eaton Commons
paragraphs: Most Eaton Commons homes are 3–4 bedrooms, 1,700–2,900 finished square feet. There's a mix of production builds and some semi-custom lots. HOA typically handles front-lawn care in the patio-home sections. Ask specifically about the phase you're looking at — some are covered by a metro district on top of the HOA.

This is a good pick for a buyer who wants Eaton's school district (RE-2) without the older housing stock of central Eaton, and doesn't need acreage. Close to Windsor and Greeley for work, and about 30 minutes from Fort Collins on a good day. If you want to see recent Eaton Commons closings alongside the current listings, I have that data.

Estes Park is the eastern gateway to Rocky Mountain National Park — a tourism town where the housing market swings between full-time residents and short-term-rental investors. Elevation, altitude, and the tourism cycle all shape what your home will do here.

sections.h2: The Housing Story In Estes Park
paragraphs: Estes Park sits at the eastern gateway to Rocky Mountain National Park, and that single fact shapes everything about living here — the views, the seasons, the economy and the housing market. It is a genuine mountain town rather than a Front Range suburb: elk walk through neighborhoods in the autumn rut, Longs Peak fills the skyline, and the nearest full-service city is a canyon drive away.

About 40 minutes to Loveland via US-34 through the Big Thompson Canyon — the nearest full-service city — and roughly an hour and a half to Denver. Worth being honest about: the canyon is a beautiful drive and it is also the only practical route east, so winter weather, rockfall closures and summer visitor traffic all land on the same road. Anyone planning a daily Front Range commute should drive it in February before deciding.

Governors Ranch is a Loveland subdivision on the south side of town, off Boyd Lake Avenue. Established mid-1990s through early 2000s, mature landscaping, and quiet streets — this is one of Loveland's earlier planned neighborhoods and it shows in the tree canopy.

sections.h2: The Housing Story In Governors Ranch
paragraphs: Most Governors Ranch homes are 3–5 bedrooms, 1,900–3,400 finished square feet, on lots ranging from 6,000 to 11,000 square feet. The HOA is active and reasonable — check the covenants before you buy if you have plans for RV parking or an ADU.

Governors Ranch competes for the same buyer profile as newer Loveland subdivisions closer to Boyd Lake, and the honest tradeoff is age vs. neighborhood maturity. If you want a bigger tree, a settled street, and don't need the newest construction, this is the answer. Compare to [Loveland's newer neighborhoods](/loveland-homes.html) before you decide.
Greeley is Weld County's seat and the largest city in NoCo east of I-25 — UNC, a substantial industrial and agricultural base, and a housing market with meaningful variation by side of town.

sections.h2: The Housing Story In Greeley For Sale
paragraphs: Greeley, Colorado, is a vibrant city with a rich history and a thriving cultural scene. As a hub of Northern Colorado, it combines urban amenities with a welcoming, small-town feel. Known for its strong agricultural roots, excellent schools, and diverse recreational opportunities, Greeley offers a dynamic lifestyle surrounded by the natural beauty of the region.
About 32 miles / 45-50 minutes to Fort Collins via US-34; about 57-63 miles / roughly 1 hour to Denver via I-25 or US-85.

Hawkstone is a Severance master-planned community — one of the largest active-build neighborhoods on the north side of NoCo. Toll Brothers, Richmond, and other national builders on lots that range from patio homes to executive builds, with a signature golf-course amenity on the east side.

Hawkstone spans a broad price range for a single neighborhood — patio homes in the low-500s to golf-course customs approaching $1M. Metro district taxes apply and matter for your monthly payment; I always run a full carrying-cost calculation before writing an offer here.

The build queue changes every quarter and so does the incentive structure — one builder will give away $30K in closing costs while the next won't move a dollar. If you're at all seriously looking here, let me pull the current spec inventory and incentive sheets across all the active builders before you tour.

Johnstown sits at the intersection of Weld and Larimer counties along I-25 — one of the fastest-growing towns in NoCo because it's roughly equidistant to Fort Collins, Loveland, and Greeley. New-build subdivisions dominate; older housing stock is concentrated near the historic core.

Johnstown, Colorado, is a charming and rapidly growing town that perfectly blends small-town warmth with modern conveniences. Mead is a small Weld County town southeast of Longmont — mostly newer subdivisions on the east side and a small historic core along Highway 66. Attractive to families who want the school district and don't mind a commute.

Mead, Colorado, is a tranquil and friendly town that captures the essence of small-town living. Set between Longmont and Loveland, it offers beautiful open spaces, a strong sense of community, and easy access to Northern Colorado’s amenities. With its peaceful neighborhoods and scenic charm, Mead is a wonderful place to call home.
About 13 miles / 18 minutes to Longmont via I-25; about 17 miles / 24 minutes to Loveland via I-25.

Milliken is a small town in southwest Weld County, just south of Windsor — growing quickly in the last decade with new subdivisions on all sides. Weld RE-5J school district, and a mix of production builds and semi-custom homes.

Milliken, Colorado, is a peaceful and welcoming town known for its close-knit community and small-town charm. Situated along the South Platte River, it offers scenic beauty, a relaxed pace of life, and easy access to nearby cities like Greeley and Loveland. With its friendly atmosphere and emphasis on outdoor living, Milliken is an ideal place to enjoy Colorado’s natural beauty and community spirit.
About 14 miles / 27 minutes to Greeley via US-34 Business; about 15 miles / 27 minutes to Loveland via CO-60.
Nunn is a Weld County town of about 500 people, north of Ault on Highway 85. Wide-open country, a strong ag base, and buyers here mostly want land and space.

Nunn is a town of about 550 people on US-85 north of Greeley, and it is one of the few places on the northern Front Range where acreage is still genuinely attainable. Almost nobody buys in Nunn for the town itself — they buy for the land: twenty, thirty-five, forty-five acres, no HOA, and horizon in every direction. That makes it a completely different purchase from a house in a subdivision, and the difference is where people get hurt.

About 21 miles to Greeley via US-85 and CR 29, and about 25 miles to Fort Collins. Both are real commutes rather than errands, and the school district — Weld RE-9, known locally as Highland — runs bus routes across 539 square miles, which tells you something honest about the distances out here.

Pierce is another small Weld County town north of Ault — school, post office, and open plains. Buyers here are typically looking for acreage or a small-town primary residence with a quick commute to Greeley or the oilfield.

Pierce is a town of about 1,100 people on US-85, sixteen miles north of Greeley and twenty-one from Fort Collins by way of CO-14. It was incorporated in 1918 and named for General John Pierce, president of the Denver Pacific Railroad, which is the reason a town this size has a Main Street at all. People buy here for the same reason they buy in Ault or Eaton — a real town with a grocery store and a school district, at a price that has not caught up with Fort Collins, and twenty minutes from a job in either direction.

16 miles to Greeley on US-85, and 21 miles to Fort Collins via CO-14. Both are genuine twenty-to-thirty-minute commutes on open road rather than stop-and-go, which is the trade Pierce offers: you drive further and you drive faster. Highland's schools are in Ault, a few minutes south, and Weld RE-9 runs bus routes across 539 square miles.

paragraphs: Red Feather Lakes is a mountain community northwest of Fort Collins in the Roosevelt National Forest — cabins, primary residences, and vacation homes at 8,000+ feet elevation. Well and septic are the norm; ask about winter road access on any listing you're serious about.

Tucked away in the Roosevelt National Forest, it’s a haven for outdoor enthusiasts with endless opportunities for hiking, fishing, and wildlife watching. Known for its tranquil lakes and rustic charm, Red Feather Lakes is the perfect escape for those seeking a quiet, nature-focused lifestyle.
About 45 miles / roughly 1 hour 10 minutes to Fort Collins via CR 74E — the primary commute route and nearest job center.

Severance is between Windsor and Eaton on the east side of the Weld/Larimer county line — one of the fastest-growing NoCo towns because it sits on the commute routes for Fort Collins, Windsor, and Greeley employers. Newer subdivisions dominate; original town core is small.

Severance, Colorado, is a charming and rapidly growing town in Northern Colorado. Known for its friendly community and scenic surroundings, Severance offers a perfect blend of small-town charm and modern development. With open spaces, great schools, and a relaxed pace of life, it’s an inviting place to settle and enjoy the beauty of Colorado living.
About 16 miles / 27 minutes to Fort Collins via CO-14.

Timnath sits east of Fort Collins on the I-25 corridor — booming with new construction, master-planned neighborhoods, and a Costco-anchored retail cluster. Fort Collins schools (Poudre R-1) in most of the town, which is a big part of the draw.

Timnath, Colorado, is a peaceful and rapidly growing town that perfectly balances small-town charm with modern living. Located just east of Fort Collins, it offers beautiful open spaces, family-friendly neighborhoods, and a strong sense of community. With its stunning views of the Rockies and easy access to outdoor activities, Timnath is an idyllic place to call home.
About 10 miles (17 min) to Fort Collins via CO-14, and about 57 miles (roughly 1 hour 7 minutes) to Denver via I-25.

Windsor straddles the Larimer/Weld county line between Fort Collins and Greeley — one of NoCo's premier bedroom communities with strong schools, several golf course subdivisions, and a mix of established and new-build housing.

Windsor, Colorado, is a thriving community that blends small-town warmth with modern amenities. Situated between Fort Collins and Greeley, it offers scenic beauty, excellent schools, and a family-friendly atmosphere. With its charming downtown, picturesque parks, and abundant recreational opportunities, Windsor provides a perfect balance of convenience and a high quality of life.
About 17 miles / 27 minutes to Fort Collins via CO-14, and about 15 miles / 27 minutes to Greeley via US-34 Business — a genuine dual-commute town.
